text.p: Consolidated Freightways Inc.'s plan to spin off some of its long-haul trucking operations will help free more its profitable units from less lucrative unionized operations, analysts said Tuesday.

Consolidated said Monday that it plans to split its long-haul trucking units into a separate company. The units, CF Motorfreight and related companies, account for more than a third of Consolidated's $5.7 billion in annual revenues but have recently been losing money.

"I think it's positive for Consolidated Freightways," said Robert Schulz at Standard & Poor's Corp., the debt rating agency. "Being a Teamster company limits the operational flexibility and the ability for the company to rigidly control labor costs."

Matt Witt, spokesman for The International Brotherhood of Teamsters, said the CF Motorfreight unionized trucking operations have hurt earnings because Consolidated has pulled cash from those operations to build up non-union businesses.

"For some years now the company has taken resources that (Teamsters) built up over many years and put them into developing and expanding non-union subsidiaries, which has been a subject of great resentment among our members," Witt said.
Nevertheless, Witt saw some benefit in the move.
"They will now have a management whose fate is tied to the same corporate future as the workers," he said.
The plan, announced after the market closed Monday, sparked a jump in Consolidated shares, which added $1.75 to $23.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Consolidated chose to play down the union aspect of the spinoff, choosing to highlight profits and losses instead.

"That particular group of companies were not valued as well as they could have been," Consolidated Chairman Donald Moffitt said in a conference call, referring to the non-union Emery air freight operation and Con-Way, a regional trucking carrier.
"It was a little confusing having two companies producing the best profits in the industry ... being clouded by the way the market was feeling towards (CF Motorfreight)," he added.
But Otto Grote, analyst at Derby Securities, said the union issues were a factor in the spinoff.
"If you spin it off, you have one business that is clearly union and all the negotiations apply to it and it leaves out the other business," he said.
In the second quarter, the unionized CF Motorfreight had an operating loss of $9.6 million on sales of $608.1 million.

For the same period, the non-union businesses that will become part of CNF Transportation Inc., Emery Worldwide and Conway Transportation Service, posted revenues of $792.9 million for an operating profit of $48.6 million.
While the companies to be spun off account for over a third, $2.1 billion, of revenues, they count for about 43 percent of the firm's 40,000 employees, with some 17,000 Teamsters.
"That would reflect the diminished productivity of the union operation," Schulz said.
CF Motorfreight President Roger Curry said plans to separate the units were in place a year ago but were postponed because a restructuring plan was not working out as hoped.
"That system is now working. That corporation will not make money this year but it is currently doing very well and is cash-positive and essentially debt-free," Curry said.
Negotiations were under way with the Teamsters to provide an incentive to boost productivity, Curry said, adding that CF MotorFreight has to improve its profitability.
"It is our intent to work with the Teamsters union for an equity incentive program," Curry said.
